issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: 'Explosion or bang sounds' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional history not represented elsewhere. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal/home-based threat, emotional closeness, family comments, shame, weakness, and hypervigilance for someone entering the home. An explosion-specific trigger pulls toward a very different trauma context and is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a distraction strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the selected items. The maladaptive strategy set otherwise reflects avoidance and conflict-generation, while the connected nodes emphasize home intrusion vigilance, bodily reenactment, shame, weakness, and loss of trust. Because Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked to Triggers and somewhat to Threat/Negative Appraisals here, a severe self-injurious coping item stands out as insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and item pattern.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking Conflict' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The patient's trauma is intimate partner physical abuse, and the other nodes describe hypervigilance, shame, weakness, loss of trust, and avoidance. Deliberately creating interpersonal conflict is a marked shift in style that is not supported by the accompanying threat, memory, appraisal, or trigger items, making this maladaptive strategy clinically incoherent in this profile.

vignette:
María was 74, a married pharmacist who had spent decades being the person others relied on for answers, calm, and competence. She came to treatment after years of carrying memories of her former partner’s physical abuse, which had begun in a period when she was already trying to keep her home steady for her family. The worst episodes were not experienced by her as a single long scene but as a series of sharp, separate pictures: the door to the house slamming hard enough to shake the walls, her body pinned in an awkward position, her face burning with shame, and the sickening sense that she could not move the way she needed to move. Because those pictures kept returning so vividly, she started to notice danger in ordinary moments that had once passed without comment; a door banging in her apartment building, a relative’s mention of family trouble, or someone leaning in with concern could suddenly feel like a warning she could not afford to ignore. Since then, comments about family could unsettle her immediately. A relative mentioning “family problems,” or even a casual remark about children and spouses, would pull her back toward those moments and make her body feel tense and ready to react, as if danger were close again. In the same way, someone getting emotionally close to her — a daughter-in-law asking personal questions, a friend trying to comfort her too directly — could stir up the old fear that closeness led to vulnerability. She had come to believe that she was no longer capable of doing the things that defined her, that she was a weak person, and that she had lost her faith in people and in the idea that life was fundamentally safe or ordered. That conviction changed what she noticed: once María had decided that danger could appear anywhere and that she could not trust her own judgment, ordinary things began to snag her attention as possible warnings — a door that shut too hard, footsteps in the hallway, a relative’s offhand comment, or someone standing too close. Once she had settled on those conclusions, staying away from gatherings, keeping conversations shallow, and stepping back from anything that might expose her became less like a choice than the only way she knew to protect herself from being hurt again.

As those beliefs settled in, María began to withdraw. She kept conversations shallow, avoided other people whenever she could, and found excuses not to join gatherings where family stories or intimate talk might arise. She also avoided paying attention to or looking at her own body; in the mirror or while dressing, she felt drawn toward what she described as the proof of what had happened to her, and she could not bear the emotional rush that followed. Allowing herself to feel anything strong seemed dangerous, so she flattened her feelings and tried to stay controlled. Yet these efforts carried their own costs. The more she held herself back, the more convinced she became that she truly was unable to do what she once did so easily, and the more certain she felt that people could not be trusted with her vulnerability. Three years of keeping away from gatherings, conversations, and anything that felt emotionally exposing had also told María something she hated to admit: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been past this by now. Each time she relied on those safety habits to get through the day, the fact that she still needed them seemed to confirm that she could not cope without them. That way of living also began to redraw what frightened her: the family questions she avoided at dinner, the personal warmth she sidestepped from her daughter-in-law, even the mirror in her bedroom all became signals of what she could no longer bear to face. Her avoidance also made family comments and emotional closeness feel even more loaded, because she had fewer ways to test whether anything could be different now.

At home, the threat never felt fully gone. She listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering her house, especially doors opening or slamming, and she remained on guard even inside her own home. The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair, and feeling that afraid day after day quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe. A front door closing hard in the apartment building or a sudden sound from the hallway could jolt her upright and send her mind back to the past. In those moments, the old memory came not as a story but as bodily re-enactment: her shoulders tightening, her chest pulling inward, her body seeming to resume the same helpless position it had taken during the abuse. The memory itself arrived in fragments, almost like a few frozen stills, each one a picture — the door, the room, the posture of fear — rather than a continuous recollection. When that happened, her body felt even more tense and ready for danger, and she became more alert at home, scanning and listening as though another blow or intrusion might follow. She interpreted the intensity of these reactions as further evidence that she was weak and that life could not be trusted. That shame deepened the memory when it surfaced again, because remembering the event brought not only fear but intense humiliation for what she felt she had endured and survived.

Over time, the cycle narrowed her life. The more María stayed away from others, the more she felt isolated and more easily startled by ordinary remarks about family or the softer emotional approach of people who cared about her. The more she tried not to feel, the more sharply the memories cut when they slipped through, and the more she noticed herself listening for doors and scanning the home. Even her work as a pharmacist, once a source of pride, felt less secure to her now; she worried that she could no longer be the steady, capable woman she had been. What finally brought her in was the realization that she was spending more and more of her day tense, listening, and pulling away, frightened that one loud sound, one personal question, or one moment of closeness would break open everything she had been trying to keep contained. She hoped for relief from the constant vigilance and shame, but she was most afraid that if she let herself trust people again, she would be hurt and humiliated all over again.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative beliefs leading to withdrawal and avoidance, but it does not clearly state that negative appraisals cause the maladaptive strategies in a causal way within the same paragraph.
The vignette describes triggers such as family comments and loud doors activating memory, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself causes new triggers or trigger sensitivity.
The vignette shows threat increasing vigilance and shame, but it does not clearly say that threat directly leads to negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
The vignette describes avoidance making comments and closeness feel more loaded, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies themselves produce triggers within the same paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows negative beliefs leading to withdrawal and avoidance, but it does not clearly state that negative appraisals cause the maladaptive strategies in a causal way within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette describes triggers such as family comments and loud doors activating memory, but it does not clearly state that the memory itself causes new triggers or trigger sensitivity.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat increasing vigilance and shame, but it does not clearly say that threat directly leads to negative appraisals in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette describes avoidance making comments and closeness feel more loaded, but it does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies themselves produce triggers within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
